Scope note. CS 474 is a computer-security course, not a cybersecurity course: it covers the machines, the software that runs on them and the data they hold. Today's network lesson looks at the network only as the path by which data reaches those machines; policies, access control and law are treated as properties of the systems and the organization that owns them.

Lesson 1 - Networks 101 for defenders: the packet's journey

0:00 - 0:14 - 14 min - Visualization (4 min): trace a customer's order on the board · Slides 4–15

Terms to learn in this lesson: network, host, packet, header, payload, IP (Internet Protocol) address, IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) / IPv6 (Internet Protocol version 6), public / private address, prefix length (/24), NAT (Network Address Translation), port, well-known port, ephemeral port, socket, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize), SYN-ACK, ACK (Acknowledgement)), UDP (User Datagram Protocol), datagram, DNS (Domain Name System), resolver, A record, TTL (Time To Live), DNS (Domain Name System) spoofing, HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) request / response / status code, cookie, HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), TLS (Transport Layer Security), certificate, CA (Certificate Authority).

Slide 4 / 56Lesson 1

Hosts, packets — and what every log line contains

  • A network connects computers (hosts) so that they can exchange data.
  • Data travels in packets: a header (addressing and control) plus a payload (content).
  • Every log line a defender reads contains an address, a port and a protocol.
My notes
Slide 5 / 56Lesson 1

IP (Internet Protocol) addresses: public, private, /24 and NAT (Network Address Translation)

  • An IP (Internet Protocol) address identifies a host’s interface; IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) addresses have 32 bits (four numbers 0–255).
  • Public addresses are reachable from anywhere; private ones (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) are never routed on the Internet.
  • /24 = 24 network bits + 8 host bits = 254 usable addresses. NAT (Network Address Translation) translates private to public and back.
My notes

Official source

  • IETF - RFC 1918, Address Allocation for Private Internets — The private address ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) used inside BlueFern's office and translated by NAT (Network Address Translation).
Slide 6 / 56Lesson 1

Ports: which program on the host

  • A port (0–65535) identifies the program on a host; servers listen on well-known ports (443 HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), 53 DNS (Domain Name System), 22 SSH (Secure Shell)).
  • Address + port = a socket. Clients use temporary ephemeral ports.
  • BlueFern’s web shop exposes five ports to the Internet; only 443 is needed.

Slide 7 / 56Lesson 1

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol): two ways to deliver

  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-oriented; the three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize), SYN-ACK, ACK (Acknowledgement)) opens the connection; delivery is reliable and ordered.
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): connectionless datagrams, no guarantee; fast — DNS (Domain Name System), time, voice and video.
  • Scanners read SYN-ACK; SYN (Synchronize) floods abuse the handshake; UDP (User Datagram Protocol) makes forged sources easy.
My notes
Slide 8 / 56Lesson 1

DNS (Domain Name System): from names to addresses

  • DNS (Domain Name System) translates names into addresses: the resolver returns the A record with a TTL (Time To Live).
  • DNS (Domain Name System) uses UDP (User Datagram Protocol) port 53 and is not encrypted by default.
  • Risks: DNS (Domain Name System) spoofing (forged answers) and look-alike names used for phishing.
My notes
Slide 9 / 56Lesson 1

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure): in the clear, and encrypted

  • HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol): request (method, path, headers, body) and response (status code, content); stateless — cookies carry the session; clear text.
  • HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) = HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) inside TLS (Transport Layer Security): encryption, server authentication (certificate from a CA (Certificate Authority)), integrity.
  • Port 80 must only redirect to 443.

My notes

Real-life example — One order, one route, five open ports

Task

Follow one customer order (ORD-1042) from a phone in a café to BlueFern Trading Inc.'s web shop, its database, the payment gateway and the warehouse, and record for every packet its source and destination socket (address and port), its transport protocol and whether its content is readable on the path; then compare the five ports the server exposes with the one port the order needs.

How it relates to this lecture

It is the concrete form of every term of Lesson 1: addresses and ports become the columns of the packet log, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) appear where they are used (the handshake for HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure), a single datagram for DNS (Domain Name System)), and HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) versus HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is shown as clear text versus ciphertext on the same route.

Where it returns in the labs / Binder

Exercise 2.1 this afternoon (draw BlueFern's network map from the profile; label the trust zones; mark three places where anything can talk to anything) and therefore Binder Part 2, due Wednesday, October 7, 23:59. The same route returns in Binder Part 4 (Class 4: the scan of exactly these five ports), Binder Part 6 (Class 6: where to place the firewall, the IDS (Intrusion Detection System) sensor and the log collector on this map) and Binder Part 8 (Class 10: the target architecture with a DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) and VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) segmentation).

A customer in a café orders a pair of hiking boots. Her phone has the private address 10.0.0.5; the café's router presents it to the world as 198.51.100.7. The browser first needs an address for the name it was given, so it sends one UDP (User Datagram Protocol) datagram to the ISP (Internet Service Provider)'s resolver on port 53 and receives 203.0.113.25 in return. It then opens a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to port 443 with the three-way handshake, runs the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake inside it, and only then sends the order - name, address, card token - as an HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) request that nobody on the path can read.

On the server the application inserts the order into MySQL on port 3306 - a conversation that should stay inside the machine at 127.0.0.1 - and calls the payment gateway over HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure). The confirmation returns over the same TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connection to the phone's temporary port 52001; a minute later the warehouse scanner on the office network, 192.168.10.40, fetches the pick list.

Then the counter-example: the same order sent to port 80. The request is identical, but there is no TLS (Transport Layer Security), and a person capturing the café Wi-Fi reads the name, the address and a card number in plain text. Nothing in the network changed; one port did. That is why the port table of the server - 21, 22, 80, 443, 3306, all open to the Internet - is the first thing a defender reads, and the first thing Class 4 will scan.

Interactive illustration — Packet Journey Tracer - a self-contained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture. The page moves a packet along a drawn route (phone, ISP (Internet Service Provider), DNS (Domain Name System) resolver, web-shop VM (Virtual Machine), MySQL, payment gateway, warehouse scanner) one step at a time. At each step it shows the source and destination sockets, the transport protocol (UDP (User Datagram Protocol) for DNS (Domain Name System), the TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handshake and then TLS (Transport Layer Security) for HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure)), what a capture on the path would see (clear text or ciphertext), and lights the row of the server's port table that the step uses. The last steps replay the order over plain HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) and expose the card data. Start / Pause lets you stop after any packet and discuss the log; Restart clears everything; Copy log, Copy code and Download packet log (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) give the students the material for Exercise 2.1. It illustrates the real-life example above and the board drawing of Lesson 1.

The Start / Pause, Restart, Copy and Download buttons inside the frame belong to the example itself; the same code is shown below and is what you download.

The code, line by line (every code line is preceded by a comment explaining what it does and why it is there)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The route is an inline SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): seven node groups (n0 to n6) with an address label each, grey links between them, and a rust circle - the packet - that starts on the phone.
  2. buildPorts() fills the port table from the PORTS list: port, transport, service, where it is reachable from, and what it should be; a wrong exposure is written in rust, a correct one in teal.
  3. Start executes one step immediately and then one every 2.6 seconds. Each step object names the origin and destination nodes, the two sockets, the transport, the application protocol, the wire view and the port-table row to light.
  4. step() highlights the origin node, moves the packet with a CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) transition, and 120 ms later highlights the destination, so the class sees the direction of travel.
  5. The packet panel is filled from the step; the wire view shows the bytes a capture would see - readable text is coloured amber as a warning, ciphertext stays grey.
  6. Steps 2-3 are the DNS (Domain Name System) query and answer (UDP (User Datagram Protocol) 53); steps 4-6 are the three-way handshake (SYN (Synchronize), SYN-ACK, ACK (Acknowledgement)); step 7 is the TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake; step 8 is the encrypted order; step 9 the local MySQL connection; steps 10-12 the gateway, the response and the warehouse.
  7. Step 13 replays the order to port 80 without TLS (Transport Layer Security): the wire view shows the name, the address and the card number in clear text, and the port-80 row lights up; step 14 summarizes.
  8. Pause keeps the index for Resume; Restart parks the packet on the phone, clears the panels and the log, and rebuilds the port table; Download writes the packet log (step, sockets, transport, application, readable) as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

Lesson 2 - Security policies: rules and responsibilities, the main types, and the ladder

0:14 - 0:28 - 14 min - Short practical (4 min): which policy is missing? · Slides 16–25

Terms to learn in this lesson: security policy, rules and responsibilities, managerial control, policy, standard, baseline, procedure, guideline, acceptable use policy, password / account-management policy, BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) and remote-work policy, data classification policy, incident response policy, purpose / scope / roles / statements / enforcement / exceptions / review / approval, acknowledgement, owner and review date.

Slide 16 / 56Lesson 2

What a security policy is — and why write one

  • A security policy is a written statement of rules and of who is responsible for following and enforcing them — not a list of settings.
  • Test: a sentence that could be pasted into a configuration file is not a policy statement.
  • Five reasons to write policies: enforcement, consistency, compliance, measurability, defence.
My notes
Slide 17 / 56Lesson 2

The ladder: policy, standard, procedure, guideline

  • Policy — mandatory and general · standard — mandatory and measurable · procedure — mandatory ordered steps · guideline — recommended.
  • A baseline is a standard for one type of system (e.g. a CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmark).
  • A document written on the wrong rung fails.
My notes
Slide 18 / 56Lesson 2

Five policy types you will meet all term

  • Five policy types: acceptable use, password / account-management, BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) and remote work, data classification, incident response.
  • Modern password rules (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B): length over forced complexity, screening against breached passwords, no forced periodic change.

Policies state rules and responsibilities; standards state measurable requirements; the settings themselves belong to procedures and baselines. Templates in the SANS (SANS Institute (SysAdmin, Audit, Network and Security)) policy library (links section) are a legitimate starting point - adapt, never copy.

Official sources

  • SANS Institute - Information Security Policy Templates — Free policy templates (acceptable use, password, remote access ...) - a legitimate starting point for Exercise 2.2; adapt, never copy.
  • NIST SP 800-63B - Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management — The modern password rules cited in Lesson 2: length over forced complexity, screening against breached passwords, no forced periodic change.
  • ISO/IEC 27001 - Information security management systems — The international management-system standard whose control 5.1 is 'policies for information security'.
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 — The Govern function is where policies live in the organizational framework introduced in Class 1.
Slide 19 / 56Lesson 2

The shape of a policy — and three failures to avoid

  • A policy has eight sections: purpose, scope, roles and responsibilities, numbered statements (“must”), enforcement, exceptions, review, approval.
  • Three failures: nobody has read it, it has no owner, it is never enforced.

Real-life example — Which policy is missing? Six situations, one ladder each

Task

Take six situations from the BlueFern Trading Inc. profile, name for each the policy type that should govern it, and write the four rungs of the ladder for it - the policy statement with its responsible role, the measurable standard, the step-by-step procedure and the guideline - then read the coverage grid to see which policy types the company needs first.

How it relates to this lecture

It applies the definition of Lesson 2 (rules and responsibilities, written) to real weaknesses, separates the four rungs on concrete text, and produces the list of policy types that Exercise 2.2 asks you to write.

Where it returns in the labs / Binder

Exercise 2.2 this afternoon (a one-page acceptable use policy and a half-page password policy for BlueFern, using the template) and therefore Binder Part 2. The standards written here return as the hardening checklist of Binder Part 5 (Class 5), the procedures as the incident plan of Binder Part 6 (Class 6), the data classification as Binder Part 10 (Sprint 2), and policies are LO (Learning Outcome) 4 material for the Final.

On Tuesday the consultant sits with the COO (Chief Operating Officer) and reads the company profile aloud, one weakness at a time. The shared administrator password: which rule would have prevented it? A password and account policy - individual accounts, no sharing, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) for administrators - with a standard of at least 14 characters, a procedure for creating and retiring accounts, and the guideline to use a password manager. The Wi-Fi password on the wall: a network and wireless access policy that separates visitors from company devices. The USB (Universal Serial Bus) drive: an acceptable use policy that forbids copying company data to personal media, resting on a data classification that calls the customer spreadsheet Confidential. The café laptop: a BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) and remote-work policy that makes the VPN (Virtual Private Network) mandatory. The ransom note that nobody knew how to report: an incident response policy. The staff photos on social media: the acceptable use policy again, with its social-media rules, and the classification that says staff roles are Internal, not Public.

Six situations, five policy types, and the two that appear most often - acceptable use and password - are exactly the two Exercise 2.2 asks you to write. The interactive example walks through the six situations, lights the coverage grid, and writes the ladder for each, so that the difference between a rule, a requirement, a step and a recommendation is visible on the same screen.

Interactive illustration — Policy Ladder Builder - a self-contained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture. The page reads six situations from the BlueFern profile one per step. For each it shows the situation, lights the governing policy type in a coverage grid (situations by policy types; a secondary type is marked with a plus sign), fills the four rungs of the ladder - policy, standard, procedure, guideline - one after the other, and logs the reasoning. At the end it counts how many situations each policy type governs. Start / Pause, Restart, Copy log, Copy code and Download coverage table (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) are provided. It illustrates the real-life example and the 'which policy is missing?' micro-activity of Lesson 2.

The Start / Pause, Restart, Copy and Download buttons inside the frame belong to the example itself; the same code is shown below and is what you download.

The code, line by line (every code line is preceded by a comment explaining what it does and why it is there)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. buildGrid() draws the coverage grid: one row per situation (its first words), one column per policy type (acceptable use, password / account, BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) / remote work, data classification, incident response, network / wireless).
  2. Start executes one step immediately and then one every 5 seconds - slower than the other examples, because the four rungs need reading time.
  3. step() shows the situation text in the rust card, converts the previous step's rust cell to teal, and lights the governing type of this situation in rust with an X.
  4. If the situation has a secondary type (situations 3 and 6: data classification), that cell is lit in teal with a plus sign.
  5. The four rungs are filled 450 ms apart: policy (rule + responsible role), standard (measurable requirement), procedure (numbered steps), guideline (recommendation); each rung turns from faded to full when filled.
  6. The log receives the situation, the missing policy type, the reason and the four rungs - the text students reuse for Exercise 2.2.
  7. finish() counts the situations per policy type and prints the ranking, then reminds the class that a policy states rules and responsibilities, not settings.
  8. Pause keeps the index for Resume; Restart rebuilds the grid and empties the ladder and the log; Download writes the coverage table with all four rungs per situation as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

Lesson 3 - Access-control principles and models

0:28 - 0:42 - 14 min - Flash-cards (4 min): the seven access-control terms · Slides 26–34

Terms to learn in this lesson: access control, subject, object, access right / permission, reference monitor, least privilege, need-to-know, separation of duties, implicit deny (default deny), model, DAC (Discretionary Access Control), access control list, MAC (Mandatory Access Control), label / clearance, RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), role, ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control), Bell-LaPadula (no read up, no write down), Biba (no write up, no read down).

Slide 26 / 56Lesson 3

Access control: subject, object, right

  • Access control grants or denies requests: a subject asks for an access right on an object.
  • The reference monitor checks every request; it must mediate every access, be tamper-proof and verifiable.
  • Access control is the technical form of authorization.
My notes
Slide 27 / 56Lesson 3

Four principles — and where BlueFern breaks them

  • Least privilege — minimum rights · need-to-know — only the information the task needs.
  • Separation of duties — no critical task by one person · implicit deny — not permitted means refused.
My notes
Slide 28 / 56Lesson 3

Three models: who decides?

  • DAC (Discretionary Access Control) — the owner decides, through an access control list.
  • MAC (Mandatory Access Control) — the system compares the object’s label with the subject’s clearance; nobody overrides it.
  • RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) — permissions belong to roles; people are assigned to roles. ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) adds conditions.
My notes

Official source

  • NIST - Role-Based Access Control project — The origin of the RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) model of Lesson 3, standardized as ANSI (American National Standards Institute) INCITS (InterNational Committee for Information Technology Standards) 359.
Slide 29 / 56Lesson 3

Bell-LaPadula and Biba: two rules each

  • Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality: no read up, no write down.
  • Biba protects integrity: no write up, no read down.
  • Secrets must not flow down; untrusted data must not flow up.

Real-life example — The role matrix and the three conflicts

Task

Build BlueFern Trading Inc.'s target role matrix (six roles against six resources, with R / W / A / -), evaluate a series of access requests against it under RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), DAC (Discretionary Access Control) and MAC (Mandatory Access Control), name the principle that decides each request, record the separation-of-duties conflicts that exist in the company today, and finish with the four rules of Bell-LaPadula and Biba on a three-level ladder.

How it relates to this lecture

It turns the four principles and the three models of Lesson 3 into decisions on concrete requests, and it shows that a matrix is not a table to fill but a set of rules to reason with.

Where it returns in the labs / Binder

Exercise 2.3 this afternoon (the 6 x 6 matrix with R / W / A / -, then the separation-of-duties conflicts) and therefore Binder Part 2. The matrix returns in Binder Part 7 (Class 7: the identity design, who gets MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) first), Binder Part 8 (Class 10: the control-to-threat table) and Binder Part 10 (Sprint 2: the insider-risk assessment), and access control is examined as LO (Learning Outcome) 1 material.

On Wednesday the consultant asks the COO (Chief Operating Officer) for the list of who may do what, and receives a shrug: everybody can read everything on the file server, both developers can reach the live customer database, the two IT (Information Technology) staff can do anything anywhere, and finance both records and approves payments. She draws the matrix the company should have. Six roles down the side: CEO (Chief Executive Officer), finance, sales, warehouse, developer, IT (Information Technology) administrator. Six resources across the top: the customer database, the web-shop admin panel, the HR (Human Resources) folder, the payment reports, the source code, the backups. In each cell, the rights the role needs and nothing more.

Then she tests it with requests. A warehouse account asks for the HR (Human Resources) folder: no entry, implicit deny. Sales updates a customer record: allowed, need-to-know. A developer reads production customer data: denied under least privilege, and recorded as conflict one, because today it is possible. Finance approves a payment it recorded: denied, separation of duties, conflict two. The administrator opens the salaries file: administer yes, read no, conflict three. The CEO (Chief Executive Officer) wants administrator rights on the backups "to be safe": denied - least privilege applies to executives, and the executive's account is the one attackers phish first.

The same requests are then replayed under DAC (Discretionary Access Control), where the owner of the HR (Human Resources) folder may grant access for the payroll run, and under MAC (Mandatory Access Control), where a Confidential label refuses an Internal clearance whatever any owner says. The last four steps place a subject and an object on a three-level ladder and apply no read up, no write down, no write up, no read down. The interactive example below runs the whole sequence; the three conflicts it finds are the three your Exercise 2.3 is expected to find.

Interactive illustration — Access Decision Simulator - a self-contained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture. The page draws the target role matrix (six roles by six resources) and evaluates twelve access requests one per step. For each request it outlines the matrix cell, names the model (RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), DAC (Discretionary Access Control) or MAC (Mandatory Access Control)) and the principle applied, shows the verdict in green or rust, marks separation-of-duties conflicts in the matrix and counts them, and logs the reasoning. The last four steps light a subject level and an object level on a three-level ladder to show the Bell-LaPadula and Biba rules. Start / Pause, Restart, Copy log, Copy code and Download matrix + decisions (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) are provided. It illustrates the real-life example and the flash-card micro-activity of Lesson 3.

The Start / Pause, Restart, Copy and Download buttons inside the frame belong to the example itself; the same code is shown below and is what you download.

The code, line by line (every code line is preceded by a comment explaining what it does and why it is there)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. buildMatrix() draws the 6 x 6 table from the M array: R, W, A or '-' per cell; an empty entry is shown faintly because it means implicit deny.
  2. Start executes one step immediately and then one every 3.2 seconds; each step object names the subject (a role, or a level for the ladder steps), the object, the action, the model, the rule and the verdict.
  3. Steps 1-6 are RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) decisions: implicit deny (warehouse - HR (Human Resources) folder), need-to-know (sales - customer DB), least privilege and separation of duties (developer - production data, finance approving its own payment, administrator reading salaries), and least privilege for the CEO (Chief Executive Officer) on backups.
  4. A step marked as a conflict colours its matrix cell in rust permanently and increases the conflicts counter - the three cells are the three conflicts Exercise 2.3 expects.
  5. Step 7 replays a request under DAC (the owner of the HR (Human Resources) folder grants access for the payroll run) and step 8 under MAC (a Confidential label refuses an Internal clearance).
  6. Steps 9-12 use the ladder instead of the matrix: the subject's level is marked in teal, the object's level in rust, and the rule (no read up, no write down, no write up, no read down) is applied.
  7. The decision panel shows subject, object, action, model, rule and verdict; the log keeps the reasoning; every decision is appended to the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) rows.
  8. Pause keeps the index for Resume; Restart rebuilds the matrix, resets the counter, the ladder and the log; Download writes the target matrix followed by the decisions as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

Reference table — Target role matrix for BlueFern Trading Inc. (Exercise 2.3) with the conflicts found today

RoleCustomer DBWeb-shop adminHR folderPayment reportsSource codeBackupsConflict in the company today
CEO (Chief Executive Officer)R-RR (approves)--Wants admin on backups 'to be safe' - refused under least privilege
Finance (3)R--RW--Records AND approves payments - separation of duties; approval moves to CEO (Chief Executive Officer) / COO (Chief Operating Officer)
Sales (12)RWRW----Can export the whole customer list - need-to-know limits exports to the data owner's approval
Warehouse (10)-R----Reads the HR (Human Resources) folder today - implicit allow on the file server
Developer (2)----RW-Reaches the production customer database - least privilege; test on a copy with fictional data
IT (Information Technology) admin (2)AAA (no read)A (no read)AA (second person)One administrator holds every right - separation of duties; content access logged and alerted; backups need a second person

R = read, W = write, A = administer, - = no entry (implicit deny). Headcounts from the company profile. 'A (no read)' means administrative rights with content access logged and alerted; with two IT (Information Technology) staff the practical control is the second person plus the log.

Lesson 4 - Legal and ethical ground rules

0:42 - 0:52 - 10 min - Fun quiz (3 min): legal or not? · Slides 35–45

Terms to learn in this lesson: computer-crime law, privacy (data-protection) law, Criminal Code s. 342.1 / 342.2 / 430(1.1) / 184, CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), Directive 2013/40/EU, authorization (written, from the owner), scope, OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) rule, personal information, PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), fair information principles, breach of security safeguards, real risk of significant harm, Law 25, confidentiality incident register, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), data subject / controller / processor, 72-hour notification, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, security.txt (RFC (Request for Comments) 9116), bug bounty, code of ethics.

Slide 35 / 56Lesson 4

Two families of law

  • Computer-crime law applies to every person: no access, interference or interception without authorization.
  • Privacy law applies to organizations: collect personal information lawfully, protect it, report when protection fails.
My notes
Slide 36 / 56Lesson 4

Computer-crime law: no permission, no testing

  • Criminal Code: s. 342.1 unauthorized use of a computer · s. 342.2 devices for that purpose · s. 430(1.1) mischief to data · s. 184 interception.
  • The unauthorized act is the offence; intent is not a defence; foreign laws (CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), Directive 2013/40/EU) apply at the same time.
My notes

Official texts

  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 342.1 (Justice Laws Website) — Unauthorized use of a computer - the Canadian offence behind 'no permission, no testing'.
  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 430 (mischief, including mischief to computer data) — Where destroying, altering or interfering with data - including a denial-of-service 'test' - falls.
  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 184 (interception) — Where capturing other people's communications on a shared network falls.
  • US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (Cornell LII) — The US (United States) federal computer-crime statute cited in the course's legal notice.
  • EU Directive 2013/40/EU on attacks against information systems (EUR-Lex) — The European framework implemented by each member state.
  • Spain - Ley Orgánica 10/1995, Código Penal (BOE) — The Spanish criminal code cited in the course's legal notice.
Slide 37 / 56Lesson 4

Three course rules — and what authorization means

  • Three rules: only the designated lab system · no OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) on real people or organizations · not sure = not authorized.
  • Authorization = the written agreement of the owner, naming the systems, the period and the permitted actions.
My notes
Slide 38 / 56Lesson 4

Privacy law: PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)

  • Personal information is information about an identifiable individual.
  • PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act): report breaches to the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada), notify individuals on a real risk of significant harm, keep records 24 months.
  • Law 25: incident register, notify the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec). GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours.
My notes

Official sources

  • PIPEDA - Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada — Canada's federal private-sector privacy law: the fair information principles and the breach-reporting duties of Lesson 4.
  • OPC - What you need to know about mandatory reporting of breaches of security safeguards — The regulator's guidance on reporting, notifying and record-keeping after a breach - the source of the lost-laptop scenario's answer.
  • Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (Law 25) — Québec's privacy regulator and the reference for Law 25 obligations (person in charge, incident register, notifications).
  • EU General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (EUR-Lex) — The EU (European Union) privacy regulation: controller, processor, data-subject rights, 72-hour breach notification.
Slide 39 / 56Lesson 4

Coordinated disclosure and ethics

  • For a flaw found without authorization: stop, record, report privately, allow time to fix, publish nothing before the fix.
  • Many sites publish a security contact at /.well-known/security.txt (RFC (Request for Comments) 9116).
  • Professionals differ from offenders by authorization and conduct.
My notes

Official sources

  • IETF - RFC 9116, A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure (security.txt) — Where a reporter finds a site's security contact for coordinated disclosure (Lesson 4).
  • ISO/IEC 29147 - Vulnerability disclosure — The standard describing how organizations receive and handle vulnerability reports (Lesson 4).
  • CISA - Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Process — How a national coordinator handles vulnerability reports - the CVD (Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure) process of Lesson 4 from the coordinator's side.
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Canada's national authority: baseline controls for small organizations and vulnerability-reporting guidance.
  • ISC2 Code of Ethics — The four canons quoted in Lesson 4: protect society; act honourably; provide diligent service; advance the profession.

Real-life example — Legal or not? Nine situations - before a test, and after an incident

Task

Pass nine situations through three authorization gates (is a real system, network or person touched? do you own it, or does a written authorization name it? is the action inside the written scope of targets, time window and techniques?) or through the privacy branch (was personal information exposed? is there a real risk of significant harm? whom must BlueFern notify, and by when?), and for each name the law that applies.

How it relates to this lecture

It makes the two families of law of Lesson 4 operational: the gates are computer-crime law applied before you act; the privacy branch is PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25 and the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) applied after something goes wrong; the disclosure path is the ethical rule for an accidental finding.

Where it returns in the labs / Binder

The gates are the scope and authorization statement you will write at the top of Binder Part 4 (Class 4) before any scan, and the rules-of-engagement discussion of that class. The privacy branch is the breach-notification mini-procedure of Binder Part 10 (Sprint 2) and the 'what to say to whom' section of the incident plan in Binder Part 6 (Class 6). The legal and ethical dimensions return in Binder Part 9 (Sprint 1) and are LO (Learning Outcome) 4 material for the Final.

Nine short stories, each a decision. A student scans the laboratory machine named in the scope document during the laboratory window: three gates passed, lawful. The same student scans the café router after class: no authorization, stop - section 342.1. A packet capture on the campus Wi-Fi "to see DNS (Domain Name System) in real life": interception, stop - section 184 and the College's own rules. A friend's verbal permission to test his employer's shop: verbal, and not the owner - stop; Annex D shows what a real authorization contains. The laboratory window has closed and the scan continues from home over the Internet: authorized target, but outside the written time and network - stop. An error page on a real supplier's site shows a database password: no authorization to go further; report to the owner, coordinated disclosure, and do not publish. A BlueFern laptop with the unencrypted customer export is lost on a bus, and three hundred of the customers live in the European Union: a breach of security safeguards with a real risk of significant harm - report to the Privacy Commissioner, notify the individuals, record for twenty-four months; notify the Commission d'accès à l'information under Law 25; notify the EU (European Union) supervisory authority within seventy-two hours. A student decides to research a real employee of a real retailer instead of the fictional BlueFern staff: stop - course rule and privacy law. And the summary: the three questions to ask before touching anything are the written scope statement of Binder Part 4.

The interactive example walks each story through the flowchart, lights the laws that apply, and starts the seventy-two-hour clock on the lost laptop.

Interactive illustration — Authorization and Privacy Gate Checker - a self-contained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture. The page reads nine scenarios one per step and lights the path each takes through a flowchart: three authorization gates leading to 'authorized work' or 'STOP - potential offence', a side path 'report, do not exploit' for an accidental finding, and a privacy branch leading to 'notify and record'. Six law tiles (Criminal Code, PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act), Directive 2013/40/EU) light when they apply, and a 72-hour clock starts for the privacy scenario. Start / Pause, Restart, Copy log, Copy code and Download verdict table (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) are provided. It illustrates the real-life example and the 'legal or not?' micro-activity of Lesson 4.

The Start / Pause, Restart, Copy and Download buttons inside the frame belong to the example itself; the same code is shown below and is what you download.

The code, line by line (every code line is preceded by a comment explaining what it does and why it is there)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. The flowchart is an inline SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): boxes for the scenario, the three gates, paper work, STOP, report-do-not-exploit, authorized work, and the three privacy boxes; edges are paths with ids so that each can be lit.
  2. Each scenario object holds the text, the list of boxes on its path, the list of edges, the box to draw in rust (a stop), the law tiles to light, the verdict, and whether the clock runs.
  3. Start executes one scenario immediately and then one every 4.5 seconds; clearAll() first removes every highlight and stopClock() resets the clock.
  4. The boxes on the path are lit 350 ms apart and the edges 170 ms after each box, so the class follows the route through the gates in order.
  5. The law tiles named by the scenario switch from faded to full; the verdict line is green for lawful and rust for a stop.
  6. For the lost-laptop scenario startClock() runs a 72-hour countdown 600 times faster than real time: one minute of the deadline passes every 100 ms, so the class sees the clock move.
  7. Every scenario appends a row (scenario, verdict, path, laws) to the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) rows and a detailed explanation to the log.
  8. Pause keeps the index for Resume; Restart clears the flowchart, the tiles, the clock and the log; finish() summarizes: two lawful, six stops, one disclosure path.

My notes

Real-life example — Placing BlueFern's controls in the cube

Task

Take the twelve controls that the BlueFern Trading Inc. plan will contain by the end of the term, place each in the cells of the McCumber cube it occupies (goal, state, kind of countermeasure), read the coverage that results, and then run one phishing attack through six layers to see which layer stops it and which layer notices it.

How it relates to this lecture

It makes the three axes of Lesson 5 concrete on real controls, shows the completeness check as a picture, and demonstrates the policy-technology pairs (the macro standard is only words until the endpoint configuration enforces it).

Where it returns in the labs / Binder

Exercise 2.1 this afternoon marks the trust zones on the network map - the first placement decision for the technology face - and the two policies of Exercise 2.2 and the matrix of Exercise 2.3 fill the policy face (Binder Part 2). The full placement is the target architecture and control-to-threat table of Binder Part 8 (Class 10), with the technology controls designed in Binder Parts 5, 6 and 7 along the way.

On Thursday the consultant lays the plan on the table as a cube. Twelve controls, one at a time. HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) on the shop: confidentiality and integrity, in transmission, technology. Disk encryption on the laptops: confidentiality, in storage, technology - the lost-laptop scenario of Lesson 4 answered. Order hashes and code review: integrity, in processing, technology and practice. Tested off-line backups: availability, in storage, technology and policy. The acceptable use and password policies of this afternoon: confidentiality and integrity, in processing and storage, policy. The role matrix: confidentiality and integrity, in storage, policy implemented by technology. Awareness training: all three goals, in processing, people - the only control that acts on judgment. Segmentation and the firewall, the incident policy, DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) protection, central logs, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) with the VPN (Virtual Private Network).

Seventeen of twenty-seven cells covered, and the empty ones are now questions instead of blind spots. Then the test: one phishing e-mail. The employee opens it - the people layer is passed. The macro standard forbids it - but a standard alone stops nothing. The mail filter has no signature for the new variant - passed. The endpoint configuration blocks macros from the Internet on a patched machine without administrator rights - stopped. The central log raises the alert two minutes later - detected. The backups were not needed. Three layers failed and the company was not harmed, which is the entire argument for defence in depth, and the interactive example shows it cell by cell and layer by layer.

Interactive illustration — McCumber Cube Control Placer - a self-contained HTML (HyperText Markup Language) page

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture. The page draws the cube unfolded as three 3 x 3 faces - one per kind of countermeasure, rows for the goals C, I and A, columns for the states stored, in transit and processed. Each of the first twelve steps places one BlueFern control in its cells (the count per cell is shown and coloured by depth), updates the coverage counter and the bar of placements per kind, and logs the reasoning with the Binder Part in which the control is designed. The next six steps run one phishing attack through six layers and colour each layer as passed, stopped or detected. Start / Pause, Restart, Copy log, Copy code and Download placement table (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)) are provided. It illustrates the real-life example and the two-control micro-activity of Lesson 5.

The Start / Pause, Restart, Copy and Download buttons inside the frame belong to the example itself; the same code is shown below and is what you download.

The code, line by line (every code line is preceded by a comment explaining what it does and why it is there)

Step-by-step explanation

  1. buildFaces() draws the three faces from the KINDS, GOALS and STATES lists; every cell has an id made of its three indexes so that a placement can find it.
  2. Start executes one step immediately and then one every 3 seconds. While idx is below twelve, step() calls place() with the next control; afterwards it calls attack() with the next layer.
  3. place() adds one to the count of every cell the control occupies, writes the count in the cell, colours it by depth (one, two, three or more controls), outlines it in rust for this step, and appends a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) row per cell.
  4. updateCoverage() counts the cells with at least one control and sizes the three segments of the bar by the placements per kind, scaled to the covered share of the cube.
  5. The log records the control, its cells, the reason it sits there and the Binder Part in which it is designed - the text students reuse for the control-to-threat table.
  6. attack() colours one layer box per step: rust when the attack passes (people, policy on paper, mail filter), teal when a layer stops it (the endpoint configuration), amber when a layer detects it (central logs), neutral when it is not reached (backups).
  7. finish() lists the empty cells and reminds the class that an empty cell is a question for the risk register, not automatically a gap.
  8. Pause keeps the index for Resume; Restart rebuilds the faces, resets the counters, the bar, the layers and the log; Download writes the placement table (control, kind, goal, state, Binder Part, reason) as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file.

  • IANA - Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry - The official registry of well-known and registered ports (53, 80, 443, 22, 3306 ...) referenced in Lesson 1.
  • IETF - RFC 1918, Address Allocation for Private Internets - The private address ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) used inside BlueFern's office and translated by NAT (Network Address Translation).
  • IETF - RFC 9116, A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure (security.txt) - Where a reporter finds a site's security contact for coordinated disclosure (Lesson 4).
  • ICANN - Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers - The organization that coordinates the domain-name system whose resolution Lesson 1 traces.
  • NIST - National Institute of Standards and Technology - The US (United States) standards body whose publications give the profession its vocabulary.
  • NIST SP 800-63B - Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Lifecycle Management - The modern password rules cited in Lesson 2: length over forced complexity, screening against breached passwords, no forced periodic change.
  • NIST - Role-Based Access Control project - The origin of the RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) model of Lesson 3, standardized as ANSI (American National Standards Institute) INCITS (InterNational Committee for Information Technology Standards) 359.
  • NIST Computer Security Resource Center - Glossary - Official definitions of access control, least privilege, separation of duties, security policy and the other terms of this class.
  • NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 - The Govern function is where policies live in the organizational framework introduced in Class 1.
  • ISO/IEC 27001 - Information security management systems - The international management-system standard whose control 5.1 is 'policies for information security'.
  • ISO/IEC 29147 - Vulnerability disclosure - The standard describing how organizations receive and handle vulnerability reports (Lesson 4).
  • SANS Institute - Information Security Policy Templates - Free policy templates (acceptable use, password, remote access ...) - a legitimate starting point for Exercise 2.2; adapt, never copy.
  • CIS - Center for Internet Security (Benchmarks) - The configuration baselines that a standard can reference (Lesson 2) and that Class 5's hardening uses.
  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 342.1 (Justice Laws Website) - Unauthorized use of a computer - the Canadian offence behind 'no permission, no testing'.
  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 430 (mischief, including mischief to computer data) - Where destroying, altering or interfering with data - including a denial-of-service 'test' - falls.
  • Criminal Code of Canada, section 184 (interception) - Where capturing other people's communications on a shared network falls.
  • US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (Cornell LII) - The US (United States) federal computer-crime statute cited in the course's legal notice.
  • EU Directive 2013/40/EU on attacks against information systems (EUR-Lex) - The European framework implemented by each member state.
  • Spain - Ley Orgánica 10/1995, Código Penal (BOE) - The Spanish criminal code cited in the course's legal notice.
  • PIPEDA - Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada - Canada's federal private-sector privacy law: the fair information principles and the breach-reporting duties of Lesson 4.
  • OPC - What you need to know about mandatory reporting of breaches of security safeguards - The regulator's guidance on reporting, notifying and record-keeping after a breach - the source of the lost-laptop scenario's answer.
  • Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (Law 25) - Québec's privacy regulator and the reference for Law 25 obligations (person in charge, incident register, notifications).
  • EU General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (EUR-Lex) - The EU (European Union) privacy regulation: controller, processor, data-subject rights, 72-hour breach notification.
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security - Canada's national authority: baseline controls for small organizations and vulnerability-reporting guidance.
  • CISA - Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Process - How a national coordinator handles vulnerability reports - the CVD (Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure) process of Lesson 4 from the coordinator's side.
  • ISC2 Code of Ethics - The four canons quoted in Lesson 4: protect society; act honourably; provide diligent service; advance the profession.
  • VirusTotal - URL check - Check any link in this module (and any download) before opening it, as the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Annex C, requires.
  • Professor Messer - free CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 course index - The official index (with runtimes) of the Security+ videos linked in Lessons 2 to 4.
  • Professor Messer - free CompTIA Network+ N10-008 course index - The official index (with runtimes) of the Network+ videos linked in Lessons 1 and 5.
  • Crash Course Computer Science #29 - The Internet (official page) - The official page embedding the Lesson 1 video.
  • Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada - Introduction to PIPEDA for your business (video series) - The official page of the short PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) explainer videos linked in Lesson 4.
  • Pearson - Computer Security Fundamentals, 4th edition (Easttom) - The publisher of the course textbook (chapter 10 and the chapter 2 network sections are this week's reading).
